cues.text: Let us now turn to Chapter 6, the 3Bells Solutions case.
This is a teaching case, and it pulls together many of the ideas we have studied about the software development lifecycle and DevOps into one story.
The case describes a software firm based in Lagos.
The firm serves a mobile banking client.
Before the intervention, the firm had two linked problems.
First, development and testing were siloed.
Developers worked in one place, and testing was done manually, separate from them.
Second, releases were ad hoc, meaning they were not planned or repeatable.
Together, these problems created security risk and outage risk.
In a mobile banking setting, a security weakness or an outage affects customers' money and trust, so you can see why this matters.
Now let us look at the intervention, the set of changes the case introduces.
I will take them in the order the source gives them.
First, Jenkins and GitHub Actions.
These are continuous integration and automation tools, used to build and run checks automatically instead of by hand.
Second, containerisation and Kubernetes.
Containerisation packages software so it runs consistently, and Kubernetes is used to orchestrate those containers.
Third, automated security checks, so that security is verified as part of the pipeline rather than left to chance.
Fourth, Git and IaC.
Git is version control for code, and IaC means infrastructure as code, where infrastructure is defined and managed through code.
Fifth, Prometheus, a monitoring tool, so the team can observe how the system behaves once it is running.
Sixth, cross-functional DevOps.
This means the work is done by teams that bring together the different skills involved, rather than in silos.
Seventh, a release manager, a role responsible for coordinating releases, which addresses the earlier problem of ad hoc releasing.
Eighth, MoSCoW prioritisation.
This is the method that sorts requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have, helping the team decide what to deliver first.
Ninth, a five percent canary release with rollback.
In a canary release, a new version is first given to a small share of users, here five percent.
If problems appear, the team performs a rollback, returning to the previous version.
Next, the pilot.
The pilot was for transaction alerts.
It used a staging environment, which is a place to test before production.
It also used manual production approval, meaning a person had to approve before the release went live.
And it used monitoring once the release was running.
Notice that even with all this automation, the pilot kept a human approval step and watched the system after release.
Now the results the case reports.
Deployment time fell from two weeks to two days.
Feedback was eighty-five percent positive.
Downtime was under zero point zero one percent.
Setup cost increased by fifteen percent.
And there was resistance to training.
So the case is honest that there were costs and people challenges, not only benefits.
An important caution.
These figures should be treated as educational claims.
They are not verified bank statistics, and they are not evidence of regulatory compliance.
Use them to learn the concepts, not to quote as real-world proof.
Finally, the lesson the case wants you to take away.
You should be able to explain why process, culture, automation and governance matter when combined.
Tools like Jenkins, Kubernetes and Prometheus provide automation.
Cross-functional DevOps teams and the release manager role address culture and process.
MoSCoW prioritisation, the staged canary release, manual production approval and rollback provide governance and control.
The case suggests that no single one of these is enough on its own.
The improvements in speed, reliability and safety came from the combination, and the setup cost and training resistance remind us that the combination takes real investment and effort to adopt.
